seoDesc: Amp to wire size: work out electrical system from the current and the source voltage. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: electrical system is what the Amp to wire size calculator works out, and it gets there from the current, the source voltage, the one-way distance and the maximum wire temperature. Think of it as a shortcut for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Amp to wire size calculator work?
sections.html:
The Amp to wire size calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports electrical system in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the conductor material); then you type in the current (I), the source voltage, the one-way distance (L) and the maximum wire temperature.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A measured quantity, entered by default in amperes. The unit chip switches it to any of the 3 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in volts. The unit chip switches it to any of the 6 supported units.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 3 options, such as copper (1.68 µΩ⋅cm), aluminum (2.65 µΩ⋅cm) and other. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in meters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in Celsius. The unit chip switches it to any of the 28 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in millimeters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.

2 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Amp to wire size calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Electrical system=allowable voltage drop (V) × source voltage × wire cross-sectional area (A) ÷ (current (I) × one-way distance (L) × (conductor resistivity, maximum wire temperature))
Wire gauge=(wire cross-sectional area (A))
Wire gauge=((wire cross-sectional area (A)))
Wire cross-sectional area (A)=(1 ÷ 4) × PI × (wire diameter (d) ^ 2)
Electrical system=(1 ÷ 4) × PI × allowable voltage drop (V) × source voltage × (wire diameter (d) ^ 2) ÷ (current (I) × one-way distance (L) × (conductor resistivity, maximum wire temperature))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Electric current – ampere, opening in amperes
  • Voltage, opening in volts
  • %, opening in percent
  • Resistivity, opening in micro-ohm centimeters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Area, opening in square millimeters
  • Length, opening in millimeters

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Amp to wire size calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the current, the source voltage and the one-way distance — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Amp to wire size calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns electrical system, derived from the current, the source voltage and the one-way distance. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Amp to wire size calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the current, the source voltage, the one-way distance and the maximum wire temperature, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter current (I) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Current (I) opens in amperes and the chip beside it offers 3 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Conductor resistivity = 0 μΩ·cm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Amp to wire size calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
